query: For high-entropy nanoalloys in high-temperature applications, what governs structural and chemical stability, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, propose a controlled comparison that would distinguish it from alternatives, predict observations relative to a baseline, define the boundaries of the prediction, identify supporting evidence from the background, and state a falsifying outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy nanoalloys used for high-temperature applications, the specific elemental composition governs structural and chemical stability by modulating the degree of lattice distortion; increased lattice distortion raises the local energy barriers for atomic diffusion, thereby reducing surface segregation and phase instability compared to alloys with minimal distortion.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy nanoalloys synthesized with controlled elemental compositions (including variations in atomic radii differences) and exhibiting a single-phase solid solution structure at ambient conditions.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the elemental composition to enhance or reduce atomic size mismatches and examine the alloys using in situ high-temperature TEM with EDS mapping under inert atmosphere conditions at 700–1000°C.
generation.conditions: High-temperature exposure (700–1000°C) in an inert atmosphere to isolate compositional effects on lattice distortion and surface segregation without interference from oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion resulting from atomic size differences among constituent elements.
generation.mechanism: Enhanced lattice distortion (driven by larger differences in elemental atomic radii) increases local energy barriers for surface atom diffusion, suppressing surface segregation and stabilizing the crystal structure at elevated temperatures. In contrast, compositions with lower lattice distortion will exhibit higher atomic mobility, leading to increased surface segregation and structural instability.
generation.predicted_outcome: Nanoalloys with greater compositional-induced lattice distortion will show fewer signs of surface segregation and maintain a more uniform crystal structure during high-temperature exposure compared to baseline alloys with near-equiatomic, low-distortion compositions.
generation.baseline: Nanoalloys with near-equiatomic compositions that induce minimal lattice distortion, expected to exhibit more pronounced surface segregation and potential phase instability at high temperatures.
generation.boundary: This prediction applies within the temperature range of 700–1000°C under inert atmosphere. Outside this range, or under oxidizing conditions, additional mechanisms (such as oxidation-induced degradation) may dominate the stability behavior.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative relationship between the degree of lattice distortion and the suppression of surface segregation is not determined; other factors such as local chemical ordering or impurity effects may also contribute to the observed stability.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of high-entropy nanoalloys: one with enhanced compositional atomic size differences (expected high lattice distortion) and one with near-equiatomic, minimal atomic size variation. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature conditions (700–1000°C) in an inert atmosphere while monitoring structural changes and element distribution in real time using in situ TEM with EDS mapping.
measurements: Quantitative analysis of lattice distortions from TEM imaging
EDS mapping for detection of surface segregation and compositional uniformity
Tracking phase stability and structural integrity over time at target temperatures
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the alloys with increased compositional-induced lattice distortion do not exhibit notably reduced surface segregation and improved structural stability compared to the baseline near-equiatomic alloys under the specified conditions, then the hypothesis that lattice distortion governs high-temperature stability would be falsified.

Here, we report on in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) observations on a DP-HEA, with a Cantor-like composition (in at.%) of Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 that comprises an fcc austenite phase and an hcp ε-martensite phase, with the objective of discerning the fundamental origin of its enhanced strain hardening and the atomic-scale mechanisms by which this occurs. We find that the strain-hardening results from the formation of three-dimensional stacking-fault networks that impede dislocation motion and further provide preferred sites for the formation of the hcp phase via a TRIP effect, phenomena that appear to be promoted by variations in local chemical composition.
